hints: Recall how solubility of Group 2 hydroxides changes from $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$ at the top to $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ at the bottom, thinking about which one forms a clear solution most easily.
walkthrough:
Picture the Group 2 hydroxides in water**
Think of stirring $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$ in water compared with $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble and gives a cloudy suspension, while barium hydroxide dissolves much more readily to give an alkaline solution. That contrast tells you the direction of the trend.
Final answer: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group.

hints: Look at state symbols in reaction 1: $\text{BaO(s)}$ goes to $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}\text{(aq)}$, so think about what happens visually when a white solid forms an aqueous solution.
walkthrough:
Read the state symbols like a story**
Reaction 1 shows $\text{BaO(s)}$ reacting with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O(l)}$ to give $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}\text{(aq)}$. You start with a white solid oxide and end with a substance in aqueous solution. In the lab you would simply see the white solid disappear as it dissolves.
Final answer: White solid disappears / dissolves to form a colourless solution.

hints: Compare atoms on each side of reaction 2: $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ to $\text{BaCO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, and ask which small molecule can supply carbon and extra oxygen.
walkthrough:
Balance atoms in your head**
You have $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ turning into $\text{BaCO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. The product contains carbon, but the starting hydroxide does not. The missing reactant must provide that carbon. Carbon dioxide, an acidic gas, reacts with strong bases like $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ to give a carbonate plus water.

hints: Recognise reaction 3 as base plus acid: $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$, so think about which cation pairs with which anion to make the salt A.
walkthrough:
Spot the neutralisation pattern**
$\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ is a base and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ is ethanoic acid. Base plus acid gives salt plus water. The $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ion needs two $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$ ions to balance charge, so A is barium ethanoate, $\text{Ba(CH}_{3}\text{COO)}_{2}$.

hints: Recall the general reaction of a Group 2 metal with water gives metal hydroxide plus hydrogen, then work out how many $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ molecules are needed to make $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Build the equation from the pattern**
Barium is a Group 2 metal, so with water it gives $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}$. To get two $\text{OH}$ groups you need two waters: $$\text{Ba} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}$$ Check atoms: one Ba, four H and two O on each side, so it balances.

hints: Recall how thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates changes down the group and which cation, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ or $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, is smaller and more polarising.
walkthrough:
Link stability to position in the group**
Thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group. Calcium is above barium, so $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ is less stable to heat and needs a lower temperature to decompose. That is why $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ breaks down first when barytocalcite is heated.
Final answer: $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ decomposes first because thermal stability of carbonates increases down Group 2.

hints: Remember each carbonate $\text{CO}_{3}$ gives one metal oxide plus one $\text{CO}_{2}$, then apply this to both carbonate units in $\text{BaCa(CO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Decompose each carbonate unit**
A single carbonate decomposes as $\text{MCO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_{2}$. Here you have two carbonates in one formula unit, so you get two oxides and two carbon dioxides: $$\text{BaCa(CO}_{3}\text{)}_{2} \rightarrow \text{BaO} + \text{CaO} + 2\text{CO}_{2}$$ Atoms balance: one Ba, one Ca, two C and six O on each side.

hints: Identify the two hydrolysable groups in B, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(CN)CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$: an ester $\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and a nitrile $\text{CN}$.
Recall that alkaline hydrolysis followed by acidification converts an ester $\text{RCO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ into $\text{RCOOH} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$.
Recall that heating a nitrile with aqueous base then acidifying converts $\text{RCN}$ fully into $\text{RCOOH}$, so think about what carbon skeleton remains when both groups become $\text{COOH}$.
walkthrough:
Map the structure of B**
Write B out fully: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(CN)CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. On the right you have a methyl ester, on the left branch you have a nitrile. Both are hydrolysed by hot $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ followed by $\text{HNO}_{3}$.

Hydrolyse the ester end**
Alkaline hydrolysis of the ester gives a carboxylate, and acidification gives the carboxylic acid plus the alcohol. So $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ becomes $\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ plus $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$. That methanol is one organic product.

Hydrolyse the nitrile end**
The $\text{CN}$ group is also fully hydrolysed under these vigorous conditions to a carboxylic acid group. So $\text{CH(CN)}$ becomes $\text{CH(COOH)}$. Combined with the other end, the carbon skeleton $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHCH}_{2}$ now carries two $\text{COOH}$ groups: $\text{HOOCCH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$, which is 2-methylbutanedioic acid.

Final answer: Organic product 1: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ / methanol
Organic product 2: $\text{HOOCCH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ / 2-methylbutanedioic acid, showing both $\text{COOH}$ groups and correct 5 carbon framework with correct valency.
